items.text: Can a linear probe on a model's activations detect misformalized Lean statements better than the model's own Yes/No answer, a Lean-only probe, or a strong LLM judge?
A probe on a 32B model's activations separates wrong from fixed Lean better than the model's own verdict, because models may know more than they say [mallen].

items.text: Probe AUROC reaches at least 0.75 on fixes made after model release, beats the model's own verdict by 0.05, and catches 25% of the strong judge's misses.
Probe gains vanish when the informal statement is removed (gap at most 0.03), or probe and judge miss the same items, as the skeptic's concern says.

Extract activations from three Qwen3-32B-family models on real and synthetic wrong/fixed Lean pairs. Train probes on synthetic data, test on real Formal Conjectures fixes. Compare with the models' own verdicts, a Lean-only baseline and strong judges.

Mallen et al. found probes usually report a model's knowledge independently of its output; Goodfire used difference-of-means from synthetic code to detect real reward hacking [mallen]. Neither tested Lean statement fidelity.

items.note: The prediction about the 32B model needs no source. The one sourced claim, 'models may know more than they say', is supported by the Mallen abstract verbatim. Caveat: Mallen's evidence comes from 'quirky' models finetuned to err when 'Bob' appears in the prompt, not from naturally occurring errors; the card's hedge ('may') is appropriate.

items.page_quote: We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.
items.note: Cited page supports that difference-in-mean probes separate true/false statements ('LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements') and transfer across datasets ('probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets'). Minor terminology difference: the paper says 'difference-in-mean', the card says 'difference-of-means'. The abstract page names no specific models; 'on Qwen3-32B' is what the plan will do, not a claim about the paper, so it needs no source.

The only checkable factual claim, 'One author wrote 268 of 515 PRs and 239 were merged in one month', carries specific values but cites no source, so it cannot be verified. items.page_quote: The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe.
items.note: Quote 'usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs' appears verbatim in the abstract. Both 'supports' claims hold: probes reveal knowledge the model does not state, and logistic regression on contrast pairs is named as the best probing method. Page: Mallen, Brumley, Kharchenko, Belrose, 'Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models'.

items.text: Do a model's hidden states for an English statement and its Lean formalization drift apart when the formalization is wrong, and is that more useful than a text judge or cheap baselines?
Expected to fail on fine-grained errors: English-Lean hidden-state similarity likely reflects only topic, as similarity alone did far worse than likelihood alone in [formalalign].

items.text: Hidden-state similarity beats the best word-overlap, embedding and likelihood baselines by at least 10 points on fixed-versus-wrong pairs and catches at least 25% of errors the judge missed.
Similarity separates matched from random pairs only (topic level), fails to beat cheap baselines on fine pairs, and is redundant with the text judge.

Compare English and Lean hidden states in Qwen3-32B, Goedel-Prover-V2-32B and Kimina-7B on 715 mined wrong-to-fixed pairs and two benchmarks, against the same model as text judge and cheap baselines [formalalign].

items.page_quote: It is calculated by taking the exponential of the average log-probability assigned by the model to each token in the formal sequence
items.note: Describes what the plan will build and measure (three models, 715 mined pairs, two benchmarks, text judge, baselines); those design choices need no source. The one cited element, the likelihood baseline, is defined on the FormalAlign page by the recorded quote (certainty score = exp of mean token log-prob). The page also defines the similarity score as cosine similarity between hidden states of informal input and formal output, matching the planned comparison.

items.page_quote: Comparison of overall alignment-selection performance across: with only the certainty score (w/ cer), with only the similarity score (w/ sim), and the complete model (Ours). w/ cer 98.98 85.64 53.69 55.55; w/ sim 45.25 20.75 20.49 21.81; Ours 99.21 85.85 66.39 66.70
items.note: All eight numbers match Table 6 exactly; columns are FormL4-Basic, FormL4-Random, MiniF2F-Valid, MiniF2F-Test, and 'Alignment Selection (AS)' is the metric ('quantifies how well a model selects the aligned formal output from multiple candidates'). On 'trained a combined certainty plus similarity scorer': the page says the model is trained with 'a dual loss that combines a pair of mutually enhancing autoformalization and alignment tasks' (cross-entropy + contrastive) and the alignment score 'combines two metrics: the certainty score and the similarity score', 'computed by taking the average' (Eq. 5). Nuance: the combination is a fixed unweighted average at inference, not a learned combiner, though both component scores come from the fine-tuned model.

items.page_quote: It is computed using the cosine similarity between the hidden states of the informal input and the formal output
items.note: Gap statement phrased as the question the plan will measure; no external factual claim and no source cited. Consistent with the FormalAlign page fetched for other items: its similarity comes from the fine-tuned model's hidden states (trained, not label-free), and its misalignments are synthetic perturbations (constant, exponent, variable_new, variable_type, equality, random pairing) rather than real research-level fixes.

scores.reason: Outcome informs whether to build probe-based auditing, but only for Qwen3-32B-family models on Formal Conjectures; link to the broad autoformalization bottleneck is indirect.
Compute is a single level (28 h) and not varied; the comparison is probe versus baselines, so the quantity measured is not compute.
Labels come from human-merged PR fixes, with a 50-triple audit. The Geometry of Truth anchor has no numeric tolerance, so exact reproduction is missing.
Prior work did not test Lean statement fidelity, and the plan states the gap: real merged fixes, beyond what the model says and beyond a strong judge.
Probe is compared with B4 (strong judge) and B1 on the same items, with numeric margins: 0.05 over B1, 25% of B4 misses, McNemar p<0.05.
No sequential dependency is removed. Data-parallel with one replica per GPU is independent copies.
restructuring.method is none, so the baseline criterion does not apply.

critique.decides_by_reason: Probe AUROC, Delta-control and B0/B1 comparisons come from S1 extraction. Only the B4 miss-catch condition needs S2, but the "style, not fidelity" failure is decidable after S1.

scores.reason: Outcomes guide whether to pursue hidden-state auditing, but only for already-found errors and a few models; failure is the more likely outcome.
Axis is model size 7 to 32B (under 10x), and the question asks about representation, not compute; bigger models also differ in other ways.
Truth is human-triaged fixes and benchmark labels independent of the method, with a CriticLeanBench anchor within a tolerance; triage is human-rated.
FormalAlign used a trained scorer; untrained similarity on research-level fixes is stated as open, though its similarity-only result is a partial prior.
Compares to best of lexical, embedding, likelihood baselines and the same-model judge on the same items with 10-point margin and 25% catch.
No sequential dependency; independent forward passes run data-parallel, one job per GPU.
restructuring.method is none, so baseline timing criterion does not apply.

critique.decides_by_reason: C1 gate at p1 stops the run if AUROC is under 0.90, a decision-rule outcome; otherwise C2 and C3 need later phases.
